title: Even the earliest unwritten traditions were already uncertain and contested
source_text: XXXVII. Sed ut clarius appareat, quam fallaces sint traditiones, quae tanquam Apostolicae extra Scripturam proferuntur, hic valde considerandum est, quod, si unquam traditiones illae certitudinem aliquam habuerunt, id maxime locum habere debuit primis Ecclesiae Christianae temporibus, quum recens adhuc erat memoria Apostolorum. At jam primis post Christum saeculis traditiones non scriptae ita incertae & variae erant, ut Doctores Ecclesiae de iis inter se certarent, & multi viri alioqui boni traditionum nomine decepti sint, & multa vana atque falsa tanquam Apostolicas traditiones sint amplexi. Ita testatur Eusebius Historiae Ecclesiasticae lib. 3. cap. ult. Papiam illum Episcopum Hierapolitanum, qui proxime post Apostolos vixit, traditionibus multum tribuisse, & inter alia scripsisse quinque libros de sermonibus Domini ex traditione non scripta, sed illos fabulis refertos fuisse. Sic quoque quum aliquanto post de celebratione Paschatis magna contentione inter Ecclesias Orientis & Occidentis certaretur, An scilicet praecise decima quarta lunae, an vero die Dominica post decimam quartam celebrandum esset: Polycrates, & alii Asiae Episcopi, qui prius illud tuebantur, traditionem Joannis & Philippi obtendebant: Victor vero Romanus, & alii Occidentales asserebant se Petrum & Paulum sequi, ut videre est apud Eusebium hist. Eccles. lib. 5. cap. 23. & seqq. & apud Socratem lib. 5. cap. 22. Ita non pauci ex antiquis existimarunt Apostolos instituisse stata quaedam & certa jejunia, hi quidem uno, illi vero alio modo. Sed Augustinus epist. 86. ad Casulanum, & Socrates lib. 5. cap. 22. negant Apostolos quicquam de jejuniis determinasse; Sed Ecclesiis liberum reliquisse quando & quomodo jejunandum esset. Et quum Augustinus in ista epistola tractet quaestionem illam, An Sabbato jejunandum sit, quod faciebant Romani & pauci Occidentales, traditionem Petri Apostoli obtendentes, reliquae vero Ecclesiae omnes aut negligebant, aut etiam illicitum ducebant, caeterorum Apostolorum, a quibus Evangelii doctrinam acceperant, traditione nitentes, judicat interminabilem esse istam contentionem generantem lites, non finientem quaestiones, adeoque ex non scripta traditione nihil certi haberi posse super jejuniorum ratione & modo. Sic etiam Tertullianus libro de corona militis, & Basilius libro de Spiritu sancto, recensent varias traditiones quas Apostolicas esse volunt, ut ex. gr. nefas esse jejunare diebus Dominicis, & iisdem diebus oportere stantes precari, ut & diebus omnibus a Paschate ad Pentecosten, quod etiam sanxit Nicena Synodus. Et tamen ista posterioribus saeculis observata non fuerunt, & pro traditionibus Apostolicis habita.
pass_a_gloss: But that it may appear more clearly how fallacious are the traditions which are brought forward as Apostolic outside Scripture, it must here be carefully considered that if those traditions ever had any certainty, that ought especially to have held in the first times of the Christian Church, when the memory of the Apostles was still fresh. But already in the first centuries after Christ unwritten traditions were so uncertain and various that the doctors of the Church contended with one another about them, and many men otherwise good were deceived under the name of traditions, and embraced many vain and false things as Apostolic traditions. So Eusebius in Ecclesiastical History book 3, last chapter, testifies that Papias, that bishop of Hierapolis who lived next after the Apostles, attributed much to traditions, and among other things wrote five books on the Lord's discourses from unwritten tradition, but that they were stuffed with fables. So also when somewhat later there was great contention between the Churches of East and West about the celebration of Pascha — whether it should be celebrated precisely on the fourteenth of the moon, or on the Lord's day after the fourteenth — Polycrates and other bishops of Asia who defended the former alleged the tradition of John and Philip; but Victor of Rome and other Westerners asserted that they followed Peter and Paul, as may be seen in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History book 5, chapter 23 and following, and in Socrates book 5, chapter 22. So not a few of the ancients thought the Apostles instituted certain fixed fasts, some in one way, others in another. But Augustine in letter 86 to Casulanus, and Socrates book 5, chapter 22, deny that the Apostles determined anything about fasts; rather they left it free to the Churches when and how fasting should be done. And when Augustine in that letter treats the question whether one should fast on the Sabbath — which the Romans and a few Westerners did, alleging the tradition of the Apostle Peter, while all the remaining Churches either neglected it or even held it unlawful, relying on the tradition of the other Apostles from whom they had received the Gospel — he judges that contention interminable, breeding quarrels and not ending questions, and so that from unwritten tradition nothing certain can be had about the reason and manner of fasts. So also Tertullian in On the Soldier's Crown and Basil in On the Holy Spirit recount various traditions they want to be Apostolic — for example that it is impious to fast on Lord's days, and that on those days one ought to pray standing, as also on all days from Pascha to Pentecost, which the Nicene Synod also sanctioned. And yet in later ages those things were not observed, though held as Apostolic traditions.
pass_b_english: If unwritten apostolic traditions ever had certainty, it should have been strongest while apostolic memory was still fresh.
Yet already in the first centuries they were so uncertain and various that Church doctors fought over them, and good men were taken in by the name of tradition.
Eusebius: Papias, living next after the Apostles, leaned hard on traditions and wrote five books of the Lord's sayings from unwritten tradition — stuffed with fables.

Pascha dispute: Asian bishops (Polycrates) alleged John and Philip's tradition for Nisan 14; Victor of Rome and the West claimed Peter and Paul for the Sunday after — Eusebius and Socrates record the clash.
On fixed apostolic fasts, ancients disagreed; Augustine to Casulanus and Socrates deny the Apostles fixed fasting rules at all.
Augustine on Sabbath fasting: Rome alleged Peter's tradition; other churches alleged other apostles — an interminable fight proving unwritten tradition yields no certainty on fasting.
Tertullian and Basil list standing prayer, no Sunday fasts, Pascha-to-Pentecost customs as apostolic — later ages dropped them even while still calling them apostolic.
